title: Digital logic
goals: Turn binary into decimal and back, and read hexadecimal
Say how many values n bits can hold
Give the output of AND, OR, NOT, NAND, NOR and XOR for any inputs
Turn a ladder rung into a logic expression, and the other way round
Say which voltages count as 0 and 1 on 5 V logic and on 24 V PLC inputs
summary:
Digital circuits work with two states: **0** and **1** (off and on, low and high).

**Binary**: each place is worth double the one to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128. Add up the places that hold a 1: 1011 is 8 + 2 + 1 = 11. A **bit** is one place; a **byte** is 8 bits, 0 to 255. **n bits hold $2^n$ values**: 8 bits 256, 10 bits 1024, 16 bits 65 536.

**Hexadecimal**: base 16, digits 0–9 then A–F (10–15). Each hex digit is exactly 4 bits, so 1011 0110 is B6. Written 16#B6 in a PLC, 0xB6 in C or Python.

**Gates**:

- **AND**: 1 only if all inputs are 1
- **OR**: 1 if any input is 1
- **NOT**: the opposite
- **NAND**, **NOR**: AND and OR, inverted
- **XOR**: 1 if the inputs differ

A **truth table** lists the output for every combination of inputs: $2^n$ rows for n inputs.

**Ladder is logic**: contacts in **series** are AND; in **parallel**, OR; a **normally closed** contact is NOT. A seal-in rung (Start OR Motor, AND NOT Stop) is a memory: a latch.

**Logic levels**: on 5 V logic, below about 0.8 V is a 0 and above about 2 V a 1. A 24 V PLC input (IEC 61131-2, type 1) reads 1 above about 15 V and 0 below about 5 V; in between is undefined, which is where a failing sensor or a long voltage drop puts it.
sources: Kuphaldt, T. R.: Lessons in Electric Circuits, Volume IV: Digital (number systems, logic gates, Boolean algebra, ladder logic)
IEC 61131-2: Programmable controllers. Part 2: Equipment requirements and tests (digital input types)
IEC 61131-3: Programmable controllers. Part 3: Programming languages (16# literals, Boolean operators)

formulas.name: Values n bits can hold
formulas.says: Each extra bit doubles the number of different values.

bench.task: In a PLC you can program offline (or a simulator), build each gate as a ladder rung and check its truth table.
check: AND: two contacts in series to a coil
XOR: (A AND NOT B) OR (NOT A AND B)
Toggle the inputs through all four combinations and write down the coil each time

cards.q: A ladder rung has two normally open contacts, A and B, in series with a coil. Which logic gate does the rung behave like?
cards.why: Power only reaches the coil if A and B are both made: AND. Contacts side by side (in parallel) would be OR.

cards.title: Binary: counting with two digits
cards.body:
Decimal places are worth 1, 10, 100…; **binary** places are worth **1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128**, each double the one to its right.

To read a binary number, add the place values where there is a 1:

1011 = 8 + 0 + 2 + 1 = **11**

A **bit** is one binary digit; a **byte** is 8 bits. **n bits hold $2^n$ values**: a byte holds 256 (0 to 255); 16 bits hold 65 536.
cards.more:
Think of a row of light switches, each labelled with its value: 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Turn some on; the number is the total of the labels that are on.

0000 0101: the 4 and the 1 are on: 5.
1111 1111: all on: 128 + 64 + 32 + 16 + 8 + 4 + 2 + 1 = 255.

Why $2^n$? One switch has 2 positions; two switches have 2 × 2 = 4 combinations; three have 8. Each switch doubles the count.

A PLC stores its inputs as bits packed into bytes and words: I0.0 to I0.7 are the 8 bits of input byte 0.

cards.q: What is binary {b7}{b6}{b5}{b4} {b3}{b2}{b1}{b0} in decimal?
cards.work: Add the place values (128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1) where there is a 1: {answer}
cards.why: Each place is worth double the one to its right, starting from 1 at the right-hand end.
cards.hint: Write 128 64 32 16 8 4 2 1 above the bits, then add where there is a 1.

cards.title: Hexadecimal: binary in short
cards.body:
Long binary numbers are hard to read, so engineers use **hexadecimal** (hex): base 16, with digits **0–9** then **A–F** for 10 to 15.

Each hex digit is exactly **4 bits**, so convert in groups of four:

1011 0110 → 1011 is 11 (**B**), 0110 is 6 → **B6**

In a PLC it is written **16#B6**; in C and Python, **0xB6**. As decimal: $11 \times 16 + 6 = 182$.
cards.more:
Hex is how status words, fault codes and memory addresses are usually shown, because each digit maps straight onto four bits: you can see which bits are on without doing sums.

The four-bit patterns are worth learning: 0000 = 0, 0001 = 1, … 1001 = 9, 1010 = A, 1011 = B, 1100 = C, 1101 = D, 1110 = E, 1111 = F.

So 16#FF is all eight bits on (255), and 16#8000 is a 16-bit word with only its top bit on: often a fault bit in a drive's status word.

Daybook's calculator takes 0x and 0b numbers and shows hex and binary for whole-number answers.

cards.q: Match each binary group of four with its hex digit.

cards.title: AND, OR and NOT
cards.body:
A **logic gate** gives an output from its inputs:

- **AND**: 1 only when **all** inputs are 1
- **OR**: 1 when **any** input is 1
- **NOT** (inverter): the opposite of its one input

A **truth table** lists every combination of inputs and the output for each. Two inputs have 4 combinations (00, 01, 10, 11); n inputs have $2^n$.
cards.more:
Say them as sentences. AND: 'guard closed AND start pressed' runs the machine. OR: 'button 1 OR button 2' rings the bell. NOT: 'NOT full' lets the pump run.

AND truth table: 00 → 0, 01 → 0, 10 → 0, 11 → 1.
OR: 00 → 0, 01 → 1, 10 → 1, 11 → 1.
NOT: 0 → 1, 1 → 0.

Every decision in a PLC program, however big, is built from these.

cards.q: A two-input OR gate has inputs 1 and 0. What is its output?
options: It depends on the last output
cards.why: OR gives 1 when any input is 1. Only 0 and 0 give 0.

cards.title: NAND, NOR and XOR
cards.body:
- **NAND**: NOT AND. 0 only when all inputs are 1; otherwise 1.
- **NOR**: NOT OR. 1 only when all inputs are 0.
- **XOR** (exclusive OR): 1 when the inputs **differ**; 0 when they are the same.

NAND (or NOR) on its own can build every other gate, which is why chips are made of them. XOR spots a difference: two switches controlling one light, or a check that two channels agree.
cards.more:
XOR is the two-way light switch on a staircase: flip either switch and the light changes. The light is on when the switches are in different positions.

In safety and monitoring, XOR does the opposite job: two sensors that should always agree are fed to an XOR; a 1 means they disagree, so one has failed.

NAND truth table: 00 → 1, 01 → 1, 10 → 1, 11 → 0. NOR: 00 → 1, 01 → 0, 10 → 0, 11 → 0. XOR: 00 → 0, 01 → 1, 10 → 1, 11 → 0.

cards.q: Two sensors on a valve should always agree: one says 'open', the other 'not closed'. Which gate gives a 1 when they disagree, to flag a fault?
cards.why: XOR is 1 exactly when its inputs differ. AND, NAND and OR all give the same output for some disagreeing pairs as for agreeing ones.

cards.title: Ladder is logic
cards.body:
Every ladder rung is a logic expression:

- contacts in **series**: **AND**
- contacts in **parallel** (branches): **OR**
- a **normally closed** contact `[/A ]`: **NOT A**

The motor seal-in rung is

```
|--+--[ Start ]--+--[/Stop ]--( Motor )--|
|  +--[ Motor ]--+
```

which is: Motor = (Start OR Motor) AND NOT Stop. The Motor contact feeding back makes it a **latch**: a one-bit memory.
cards.more:
Read the rung left to right as power flowing. Power reaches the coil if it can get through Start or (in parallel) the Motor contact, and then through the Stop contact, which conducts while Stop is not pressed.

Once Motor is on, its own contact holds the branch made, so releasing Start changes nothing: the rung remembers. Pressing Stop opens the series path and the memory is lost: Motor goes off and its contact opens.

In Structured Text the same rung is one line: `Motor := (Start OR Motor) AND NOT Stop;`

cards.q: Match each ladder pattern with its logic.
pairs: A coil's own contact in parallel with Start

cards.title: What voltage is a 1?
cards.body:
Real signals are voltages, so each family of logic has **thresholds**:

- **5 V logic** (TTL levels): below about **0.8 V** is 0; above about **2 V** is 1
- **3.3 V** microcontrollers: roughly below 0.8 V is 0, above 2 V is 1; check the datasheet
- **24 V PLC inputs** (IEC 61131-2, type 1): above about **15 V** is 1; below about **5 V** is 0

In between is **undefined**: the input may read either way, or flicker.
cards.more:
The gap between the thresholds is a safety margin against noise: a 0 that picks up a volt or two of interference is still a 0.

Trouble comes when a signal lands in the gap. A failing 24 V sensor that only pulls its output up to 12 V, or a long run of thin cable with a big voltage drop, gives an input that reads 1 one scan and 0 the next.

Measure it: a healthy PNP sensor output reads close to 24 V when on and close to 0 V when off. Anything in the middle is a fault to chase, not a setting to change.

cards.q: A 24 V PLC input's LED flickers. A meter on the input reads 10 V with the sensor on. What is happening?
options: 10 V is in the undefined band, so it reads either way
10 V is a clear 1 on a 24 V input
10 V is a clear 0 on a 24 V input
The input card counts volts, not 1s and 0s
cards.why: Type 1 inputs need about 15 V for a 1 and under about 5 V for a 0. 10 V is in between, so the input may read either way and flicker. Find out why the sensor's output is so low: a failing sensor, a bad connection, or a big voltage drop.

cards.q: A drive's status byte reads binary 1011 0110. What is it in decimal and in hex?

steps.ask: Write the place values over the bits.
Split into groups of four for hex.
Each group as a hex digit.

cards.why: Decimal by adding place values; hex by groups of four. Check: $11 \times 16 + 6 = 182$.

cards.q: Why does step 3 split the byte into groups of four bits for hex?
cards.model: Sixteen is 2 to the power 4, so one hex digit holds exactly the 16 values that four bits can make. Each group of four bits therefore turns into one hex digit on its own, without carrying anything to its neighbour. That is what makes hex a quick shorthand for binary: you can read bits straight off each digit.
points: One hex digit per four bits

cards.q: Turn 200 into 8-bit binary.

steps.ask: The biggest place value that fits: 128. Take it off.
The rest are 0. Write it out.

cards.why: Take off the biggest place value that fits, write a 1, carry on down. Check: 128 + 64 + 8 = 200.

cards.q: How many different values can a {n}-bit number hold?
cards.why: Each bit doubles the count. The biggest value is one less, because counting starts at 0.

cards.q: A NAND gate has inputs 1 and 1. What is its output?
cards.why: AND of 1 and 1 is 1; NAND inverts it to 0. Every other input combination gives a NAND output of 1.

cards.q: Converting 0110 1001 to decimal. One line is wrong. Which?
cards.why: The last bit is the 1s place, not the 2s. Read the place values right to left from 1. Check with hex: 0110 = 6, 1001 = 9, $6 \times 16 + 9 = 105$.

cards.q: What is the largest value an unsigned {n}-bit number can hold?
cards.why: There are $2^n$ values, starting at 0, so the largest is one less. (A signed INT uses one bit for the sign: −32 768 to 32 767 for 16 bits.)

cards.q: A rung has contact A in parallel with contact B, then in series with a normally closed contact C, to a coil Q. Which expression is it?
options: Q = (A OR B) AND NOT C
Q = A AND B AND NOT C
Q = A OR (B AND NOT C)
Q = NOT (A OR B) AND C
cards.why: Parallel is OR, so A OR B; then in series (AND) with a normally closed C (NOT C). The brackets matter: the OR is done first because both branches feed the same series contact.

cards.q: A logic function has {n} inputs. How many rows does its full truth table have?
cards.why: One row for every combination of inputs: $2^n$.

cards.q: A fault code reads 16#{h1}{h0} (both digits 0–9). What is it in decimal?
cards.why: In hex the left digit counts sixteens, not tens. Reading 16#25 as twenty-five is the classic slip: it is 37.
cards.hint: The left digit is worth 16 each.

cards.q: A machine must run only when the guard is closed and either of two start buttons is pressed. Which logic?
cards.why: 'And' between the guard and the start condition; 'either' between the buttons is OR. Needing both buttons would be AND; the guard must be closed, not NOT closed. (A real guard interlock is a safety function, not ordinary logic.)

cards.q: Match each reading with what the input sees.
pairs: 23 V on a 24 V PLC input
1 V on a 24 V PLC input
10 V on a 24 V PLC input
3.2 V on a 3.3 V logic input

cards.q: Two contacts in parallel, feeding a coil. Which gate?
cards.why: Power can pass through either branch: OR.

cards.q: Binary {b3}{b2}{b1}{b0} in decimal?
cards.why: Add the place values of the 1s.

cards.q: Match each gate with when its output is 1.
